title: Spike damping shadow-run notes
content:
Goal: quick field notes from shadow-run experiment to evaluate a lightweight "damping" admission-control layer that attenuates short high-amplitude spikes without impacting steady-state latency. This is a personal scratchpad; rough numbers and preliminary conclusions.

Background/context:
- Problem observed in prod-sim tests: sudden 10–20s bursts from client-side fanout cause p99 spikes > 2.2s on small models (chat-7B-quant). Upstream autoscaling cannot react fast enough; we want a cheap in-runtime mitigation.
- Idea: transiently reduce accepted concurrency for a short window (20–200ms) when instantaneous queue depth jumps above threshold, while allowing a fast bypass for small payloads and warm-cache hits.

Test harness and environment:
- Date: 2025-01-08 -> 2025-01-11 (multiple runs).
- Cluster: dev-dedicated-3 (4x A10G equivalent), single region us-west2, 8 replicas of worker process.
- Model: chat-7B-quant (4-bit q4m-like profile), kv-cache enabled.
- Runtime: serving-runtime v0.22.1 with kernel selection heuristics on.
- Load generator: custom script (burst-mixer) that composes Poisson baseline (qps=120) + spike bursts (250–800 qps for 200ms–3s). Payload size: 64 tokens prompt / expected 128 tokens gen.
- Measurement: client-side histograms, disaggregated by warm/cold cache, by batch-size, and by priority lane. We record p50/p95/p99, mean latency, observed QPS, and KV cache hit rate.

Admission-control (damping) configurations tested:
- D0: baseline (no damping) 
- D1: conservative damping: threshold q=250 instantaneous queued requests -> drop window 200ms, reduction factor 0.5 (accept only half of admits), bypass for warm-cache & size<64 tokens
- D2: aggressive damping: threshold q=150 -> window 100ms -> reduction factor 0.33, no bypasses
- D3: adaptive-timeout: threshold q=200 -> window proportional to excess (excess_ms = min(500, 50 * excess_q)) -> bypass for warm-cache

Representative runs (aggregate summaries):
- R1 (D0 baseline): baseline + spike (burst 800qps for 500ms). Observed: p50=34ms, p95=290ms, p99=1.9s, mean latency=210ms, QPS sustained 142. KV-hit overall 68%. Tail dominated by cold-cache large batches and queueing.
- R2 (D1 conservative): same burst. Observed: p50=36ms, p95=220ms, p99=1.1s, mean=180ms, QPS 120 (drop of ~16%). KV-hit 71%. Notable: fewer huge batches, average batch size down 12%.
- R3 (D2 aggressive): same burst. Observed: p50=40ms, p95=260ms, p99=900ms, mean=205ms, QPS 96 (big throughput loss). KV-hit 65%. System underutilized between bursts due to over-throttling.
- R4 (D3 adaptive): burst varied lengths 200ms, 1s, 3s. For short bursts (200ms) p99 ~480ms, mean 170ms, QPS drop 9%. For long bursts (3s) p99 800ms, mean 200ms, QPS drop 12%. Overall best tradeoff across durations.

Per-run observations and heuristics:
- Small payload bypass is crucial: when we allowed warm-cache & small payload bypass, many short-turn requests got fast paths and p95 improved without cost to throughput.
- Aggressive fixed reductions avoid tails but harm steady-state utilization — bad for cost.
- Adaptive window that scales with excess queue depth (D3) smooths out short spikes while backing off when bursts persist; it reduced p99 by ~55% vs baseline for 500ms bursts with only ~10% throughput loss.
- KV cache hit rate changes are subtle but matter: slightly higher hit rate with damping (reduced churn) helps latency.

Quick micro-profiling notes:
- Under heavy bursts, we observed spike in kernel-switches in worker process (syscall backoff) — maybe from scheduler preemption when batches pile up. Need perf capture of kernel wakeups.
- Batch assembler latencies increased when queue depth jumped; reducing max_batch_wait_ms from 40 -> 20ms reduced worst-case batch formation delay but increased average batch fragmentation.

Immediate action items / TODOs:
- (T1) Add a low-cost telemetry event for damping decisions (timestamp, excess_q, window_ms, decision) to infra telemetry pipeline. Want to correlate decisions with observed p99. Assigned Mira.
- (T2) Run D3 across quantized 13B variant and in a larger cluster (dev-dedicated-7) to verify behavior scales. Assigned Liam.
- (T3) Perf capture of worker syscall wakeups during a synthetic long burst (3–5s) to understand kernel-level latency spikes. Self-assign.
- (T4) Explore rule: bypass for requests with cached prompts (KV-hit recent) + tokens_out < 64. Quick A/B to test.

Open questions / caveats:
- Real client behavior has correlated retries; our generator currently does not emulate concurrent retry storms (needs next iteration). That could change tradeoffs because damping may increase perceived failures -> retries.
- Need to reconcile with existing circuit-breaker/fallback policies in console rollouts; damping layer could interact unpredictably with canary failover.
- Cost model: rough calc shows D3 saves tail related SLO penalties but reduces billable tokens by ~8–12% (lost QPS). Need product input on acceptable tradeoff.

Short conclusions (scratch):
- Lightweight, adaptive damping (D3) looks promising for short-duration spikes: cuts p99 by ~40–60% on mid-length bursts with single-digit to low-teens percent throughput hit.
- Fixed aggressive throttles are simple but too costly in steady state.
- Immediate next step: telemetry + run on 13B quant to validate.

Notes to self: keep this informal. If we formalize for infra/playbook, move cleaned numbers into a spreadsheet and add run-ids/time-series traces. Also prepare a short demo script (2 slides) for ops to show effect on p99/p95 next ops sync.

Raw run ids: run-20250108-0143-D3, run-20250109-0932-D1, run-20250110-1817-D2

End of scratchpad.
